The first experience: Another Shinkasen rushing past our platform at full speed. Oh man, what a performance. Within a fraction of a second the rather long train rushed past.Second experience: the journey itself. Green Class, wide seats, backrest that can be lowered far. Clean. Quiet ride, hardly any shaking as one crossed. Just like on rails. With a sushi bento box from the platform kiosk, we flew past Mount Fuji and many villages. A highly recommended experience!
Punctual, clean and fast. Also, phone works well while riding. My proof being that I'm writing this on a Shinkansen. So meta.

Need to find lots of readings on net, to know tht it's not operated by East JR, but by Central rail instead, such that u can't purchase a ticket from the popular East JR site, nor the Central rail site (since u need their credit card). Purchusing a ticket at Shinjuku station for a ride is more simple than purchasing a ticket at Tokyo station (where you board). Well...
We took the train back from our day tour to Mount Fuji . It was a great experience and only took us 40 minutes to get back to Tokyo. Extraordinary experience.

That was a unique experience! The Shinkansen train runs so smoothly! Unbelievable speed! That was a real dream! The train is also very clean and there is a lot of space on the seats, the leg room is perfect! You have to experience this in Japan.

The best way to travel between each major city is the Shinkansen. Always on time, super clean, smoking room, perfect toilets as well as sinks and mirrors... I took it 3 times, to travel from Tokyo to Osaka. Ultimately it's an activity, an experience, even an attraction... What a pleasure, comfortable seat, clean tablet. Tea or coffee trolley service with charming and friendly staff. That's a change! just for that, I will live in Japan!!!!

We would all have heard of the fastest train in the world at some point. This time I had the opportunity to board to Kyoto from Odawara station. The speed inside the train is not felt! But from the outside it can only be seen for a few seconds. The seats are comfortable and have super legroom. If you need to go from point A to point B in Japan, it is undoubtedly an excellent option to move: Tip: Select seats (from Tokyo to Kyoto on the right side of the train to see Mt. Fuji (in a train with 3-2 configuration; select seats D or E))

Surprisingly, there are no souvenir shops or restaurants inside the ticket gates at Tokyo Station on the Tokaido Shinkansen, just the standard shops and ekiben shops. Be sure to finish your shopping inside the ticket gates of conventional lines at Tokyo Station. Also, the non-reserved seats near the last train get extremely crowded, so be sure to get a reserved seat. The inside of the train has large windows, so you can enjoy various scenery such as Mt. Fuji, Tokyo Tower, and the five-storied pagoda even from inside the Shinkansen! And after all, the Shinkansen is cool! It has always been a dream vehicle for children!

We took the bullet train from Tokyo to Kyoto, a past capital of Japan.  150 to 200 mph, was a fast trip under any consideration. Good seating, clean and was worth the trip for sure.  This is a must for anyone traveling to Japan.  A little pricey, but how often do you do this?  On a clear day, you will get a good view of Mt. Fuji.  Fun event?

Shinkansen is very fast and efficient ride through Japan. Almost always on time and you can trust this bullet train. If you are not Japanese, you can buy "JR pass" before you leave your country and buy this pass. There are two kinds: 2-week pass and 3-week pass. You can ride all Japan Railway and JR bus during that period. It is great for Shinkansen because you can have reserved seats with no extra costs. Please see JR website for detailed information. Anyway, Japan Railway is one of the best, fastest, and trusted railway in the world.

We used the skinkansen bullet trains from Tokyo Station to both Kyoto and Nagano for the snow monkeys.  The trains are indeed clean, including the restrooms, as everyone on TripAdvisor raves.  There is a lot more room than on a plane as well.  Food is served eventually but you have to catch the vendor as they do move fast through the cars.  If you stop them they will help you find something on their cart that you like.  Many people, including us, brought their own food as well and that is perfectly OK.When the trains arrive at Tokyo Station they are all emptied and then a cleaning crew boards and spends about 10 minutes doing their thing.  They will then exit the train and the doors will close.  Then a few minutes later the doors will open and you will have a few minutes to board before the train leaves.  So, the message is that you have to be waiting on the platform outside your car number.....the car numbers are given on overhead signs.  If you don't have a car number on your ticket, you can board anywhere and wait for the announcement of which cars are for open seating....it's usually #2-3-4.  Do understand that if you are not waiting at your car when the doors open, you may miss your train.  So in winter, and with wind, it can be uncomfortable waiting in the cold.....but you have to do it.....everyone does. The trains are fast, clean, and on time.  Can't ask for anything else really.....
Here we experienced fast trains in the Japanese effect. Accurate system, trains arrived 1-2 minutes before and left the station precisely. Comfort inside, large legroom, quiet, good seats, etc.
Super nice trains with a high standard. With a Rail Pass, it's a convenient way to travel around Japan. Can really be recommended.

If you are in Japan for an extended period and want to travel parts of the country the JR Rail pass is a really great deal, we took the green car kind of like of business class and it was great, bring your own snacks are there stuff is mediocre and the trains are like clock work you need to pay attention to go on the right train and switching trains .... also some of the stations are huge so give yourself enough time to orient yourself ...they have overhead racks for your luggage as well, I highly recommend the JR pass !!!

Had a spare day in Tokyo, right at the start of Cherry Blossom time.Where else would you want to go but Kyoto. Without the train, no chance at all.Takes 2 hours 20 minutes including stops.A train leaves basically every 10 or so minutes. Staggering.Lash out and pay the extra Yen 500 for a reserved seat. At least you get to sit for sure where you've booked and not enter a bun fight as peopl scramble for the non-reserved section.Left around 9am did the 450 kilometers and on a bus to the golden temple by 11.30. Just brilliant. Then over to Gion, at this time of year fantastic, back on the 5.30 back and in hotel by 8pm. Just too easy.Finally, Kyoto transport, how good are the buses? Flat fee of Y230 on each route, no matter how far you go, AND if you don't have the right change there's a machine which will change your money next to the driver. Again, why can't we have this?The only downside of the day was could not see Mt Fuji at all. It was pretty clear, there were other snow capped mountains to snap, but the big boy must have been on vacation.

Took the Shinkansen to Kyoto.  This was the best train ever and I have taken many.  Not only is it super fast and surprisingly on time, but is is amazingly clean.  The service is great and ladies, you will appreciate this, the bathrooms are spotless.  Spend the little bit extra and go for the green car (first class).

The main line of Japan's proud Shinkansen network. As someone who lives in Tokyo, I naturally have different preferences when it comes to Kansai and Nagoya areas, but Hiroshima is far away from the airport.

We planned a trip to Kyoto on this amazing train from Tokyo as we had heard it was an amazing experience and it was true! This was just the most exhilarating train ride I have ever been on, its slick service and futuristic platform started to make it feel more like a flight, and did it fly! We past Mount Fuji which was a great clear view, and wizard past all the stations, it left on time and arrived on time and was worth every penny! Puts our rail service in U.K. to shame, it's a must, easy to purchase tickets and everything at the station in English, you can't go wrong!

I have travelled on Tokaido, Sanyo, Hokuriku and Tohoku Shinkansen. The experience was amazing and cannot be found in other countries.Trains are stable, clean, spacious and fast (up to 320 km/h). Standard class is in 3+2 seat arrangement. Seats are all face to the direction of the train to avoid motion sickness and they can be rotated backward if you have got 4 or 6 persons traveling together. Leg rooms in standard class are big enough and even much better than traveling on an airplane.For services, there are assistances on train selling drinks and bento box. They bow after entering and before leaving train carriages. Announcements are in both Japanese and English (Mandarin and Korean are available on major stations of Kyushu Shinkansen as well). Trains are on time. The only time I faced delay was because of strong wind. There are Reserved and Non-Reserved seats available.Traveling on the Shinkansen is pretty easy. Remember to buy a normal ticket and an additional Limited Express Ticket and pass through ticket barrier twice if the station is served by both local trains and Shinkansen.If you travel on the long distance Shinkansen at least twice, make sure to buy a Japan Rail Pass or Regional Rail Pass (in Kansai or Kanto areas). For JR Pass holder, please note it is not available on Nozomi trains on the Tokaido Shinkansen.

I used it between Nagoya and Tokyo. I took the Nozomi train to get there because I was concerned about time. I had purchased E seat on the mountain side in advance. The weather was good and Mt. Fuji looked beautiful. Mt. Fuji can be seen from the sea side. From Tokyo, it's after leaving Shizuoka Station, and from Nagoya, it's just before Shizuoka Station. I was impressed when I saw it for the first time. Don't think you can't see Mt. Fuji because you're in A seat, but if the weather is nice, why not look out the window. On the way back, I rode the Kodama. That's because there is a great value travel product called "Plat Kodama." "Plat Kodama" is a recruitment-organized trip organized by JR Tokai Tours and is not a "ticket." Therefore, there are various restrictions and you need to be careful, but the appeal is that it is cheaper than usual. Normally 8,100 yen (8,300 yen from April) between Nagoya and Tokyo. During busy seasons, the price increases by 1,200 yen. This price also includes a voucher for one drink. (However, "Kodama" is not sold on the train, so you must exchange it at the station store where the exchange store sticker is affixed.) You can also ride the Green Car for an additional fee. An additional charge of 1,000 yen is required between Nagoya and Tokyo. It's a ``Kodama'' so it takes some time, but it's nice to enjoy a leisurely Shinkansen trip.

I rode between Tokyo and Shin-Osaka. It was my first time riding the Shinkansen with my one-and-a-half-year-old child, so I was nervous, but everything turned out okay. My son, who loves trains, was in a good mood as he was enjoying the scenery from the Shinkansen and was happy to see so many trains. This time, I didn't have to change diapers even once on the round trip, but I think if they could add one more multi-purpose room, the number of people traveling with children would increase. I think so.

The Japanese train can get on even if you go home at the departure time. The Shinkansen departing 09:00 departs between 09:59. Be sure to be on the platform several minutes before getting on the train. For some reason, the Shinkansen will depart at this number of seconds 00, 15, 30, 45. The train is departing though it is not 09: 01.There is a person who is stomping with a stationer but can not ride.Please display one minute earlier.Japanese trains allow you to catch the train even if you go to the platform at the departure time. If the Shinkansen departs at 09:00, it will depart between 09:59 and 09:59. If you are boarding a train, be sure to be on the platform a few minutes early. The reason is that Shinkansen trains depart at the following seconds: 00, 15, 30, and 45. The train is leaving even though it's not yet 09:01. There are people who can't get on the train and are fighting with the station staff. Please move the display forward one minute.

The speed is a chapter by itself, which I do not have to mention. Seats and especially the space between the rows is fantastic. I don't think anyone can't fit their knees - not like in aeroplanes. It travels fast and very smooth with the landscapes passing by.

The Tokaido Shinkansen operates on a minute-by-minute schedule similar to that of commuter trains. The terminal station is directly connected to JR's conventional lines, so if you arrive 5 minutes early, you can board without any problems. On this day, I took a train from Shinagawa to Nagoya, and although the ride time itself is longer than that by plane, considering other times, I think the Shinkansen would be more efficient for getting to Osaka. Even the regular seats have a wide space between seats and can be reclined without hesitation. Even so, the Shinkansen is a cash cow, with so many trains running and so many people riding them all the time.

What more can you say - super fast, super comfortable, good amenities on board, super punctual, and super polite staff. In Japan - the best way to travel especially between Tokyo and Osaka. Only drawback is the price - a trifle expensive.

This time, I took a trip on the Kodama train, which stopped at every station. I thought that the stations that I usually pass by in the blink of an eye on the Nozomi train had a more elegant feel on the local train. At each station, I would be overtaken by one or two Nozomi and Hikari trains, so the stops were long and boring, but I thought it would be nice to take a trip like this once in a while.
Was just on the train from Tokyo to Kyoto, I highly recommend it, especially the "Green" car... no smoking.
This is not the Shinkansen I rode, but the Hikari train on the platform across the street. Today I will be riding the Nozomi train on a business trip to Tokyo. Nozomi has been quite crowded lately.

There are many office workers in the morning and evening. There are a lot of trains, so I feel like I can ride if I go, but I always make reservations anyway. It may take some time to travel between Tokyo and Osaka, but I think it's more convenient than flying. I wish the price was a little lower.

RAGE|Rave.view		NAME:	Tokaido Shinkansen (Bullet Train service)	LOCATION:	Japan	TIME OF YEAR:	March 13	RATING:	5/5	PRICE:	Included with tour	RESERVATION:	n/a	QUALITY:	Fast	LENGTH:	Felt like 0 minutes (was way faster than any train I've ever been on)	RAVE:	Super fast and super smooth	RAGE:	Eerily smooth for such high speeds?	LOWDOWN:	This was part of our week long Golden Route Cherry Blossom tour with All Japan Tours. The trains soared through the station at super high speeds (300 km/hr or 185 miles/hr). When we finally got on our train I underestimated the smoothness of the ride. It  felt like we weren't even moving! Amazing and efficient. I now weep on the subways of NYC.	RAGE|Rave.view

The Shinkansan, which probably means something like 'new line' which started in 1964, the year of the Tokyo Olympics is a high speed 'bullet train' that now operates all over Japan.The Tokaido Shinkansen is the train that runs between Tokyo and Osaka and beyond.They operate up to 320 KM per hour although can go faster.They are clean and quiet. For overseas visitors it is wise to purchase a JR Pass in your country of origin, have it validated in Japan as you will save money.Particularly around Tokyo you will see a Shinkansen on the over head rail lines every few minutes and they are quite impressive.

The shinkansen experience we had from Kyoto to Tokyo was tremendous!! It started from purchasing the tickets, where there was a separate line for foreigners, and a translator came to help us arrange for the tickets and seats. The train is very spacious, and everyone was curtious towards us even with our large suitcases. A bit on the pricey side but well worth it!!*Please note there is enough space at your seat to place a large suitcase though it may roll around and block the inner seats accessibilty. There is also limited space at the end of the car behind the last row is seats too

The best thing about Japan is its high-speed trains, known as Shinkansen. With the JR Pass you can travel on most lines without paying or making reservations, but it's always a good idea to check before getting on the train.

I purchased a 1 week rail pass and it allowed me to travel from Tokyo to Osaka, Kyoto and back.  It's the best and fast way to travel in Japan and to see the country side.  The train goes extremely fast and you can't even feel the speed.  It was a fun and amazing experience and can't wait to experience the bullet train again.

We travelled from Tokyo to Kyoto and then did a return trip Kyoto to Hiroshima and then back to Tokyo . It is an amazing service. . We only reserved seats at the terminal before we departed . So easy . If it's a busy time you can reserve ahead or in our case one section we just walked on to the cars that are for those without a reserved seat . We loved that we caught sight of Mt Fuji from our window. The trains are  so comfortable , quiet and so clean . They offer food and beverage to buy on every trip .  Best way to get around.
Safe and fast. Precise and comfortable. The best in the world. You can enjoy your trip in Japan. Recommend.
I rode the Kodama, which I don't usually ride. The station I got off at was "Gifu Hashima", but since "Kodama" doesn't run very often, I feel like it might be a bit inconvenient to use.

The accommodation for this trip is Shin-Yokohama. There are things I want to see and places I want to go to in Tokyo, so I thought about how I would go. If we were to take a regular train, it would be a hassle to change trains, so we bought two sets (12 tickets) of Shinkansen tickets for three people, which was a little expensive, but if you think of it as leisure, it's fun. I arrived at Shin-Yokohama Station stress-free.
I often travel between Tokyo and Himeji on business, but since it's inconvenient to fly from Himeji, I always take the Shinkansen. Even Nozomi gets tired after riding for nearly 4 hours.

Before I start I would advice travellers to get a JR pass. I got mine for 7days which was $330 AUD or so.The trains are not like your average trains. Planes aren't even on this level. Seats are comfortable with a lot of leg room. The scenes you get from traveling on the train is memorising! It's a good way to tour the country and experience their culture but without moving.

Very positive experience travelling on the Shinkansen from Tokyo to Osaka and then return. The bullet train is punctual, clean and spacious inside. We chose the bullet train over a plane due to the convenience- no need to trek out to the airport, check in your baggage etc. We chose the Nozumi line which is the express and takes 2hrs, 30mins for the one way journey. You can take large suitcases with you on the skinkansen and leave them behind the last row of chairs on your car (carriage). You are able to purchase your tickets on the day and select the next departing Shinkansen. To my surprise they leave very frequently- generally a few within an hour!!!

tip: Book a train 1 day before you departure or else you will left with individual seats.I am travelling with kids and travelling from shin hakodate to Tokyo station. we where told that we that we cant sit togther as there where no space. we are travelling with 2kids and we have bought three adult tickets and all seats were seperated. we went down at the next station to change hoping that we can buy a ticket that can sit together but was told that the next few trains have no space. all seats are individual. I wasnt expect this kind of service rendered with such reputable train provider. what a disappointment!

The Shinkansen that runs from Tokyo to Shin-Osaka has stations called ``Kodama'' and limited express trains called ``Hikari'' and ``Nozomi.'' The number of trains is higher than other Shinkansen trains, and the price is also cheaper than other Shinkansen trains.
Clean, punctual, easy to use, fast, comfortable... all in all this is how trains should be. A fantastically easy way to get around...

Since I usually travel alone, I reserved seat A, which seats 3 people by the window. As others have written, if there are three seats, there is a high possibility that the middle seat will be empty. However, last time, when I heard the cheers, I looked over and saw that Mt. Fuji was clearly visible on the other side. I didn't expect it to look that big, and it's especially beautiful in winter. Everyone was taking pictures, but I was sitting in the farthest seat and couldn't move... This time, I reserved the E seat by the window for two people. I was fully prepared and was able to take the photo this time. The weather is nice and I'm very happy. However, the seats in the Sakura in Western Japan are as comfortable as the green cars, even in regular cars, so I would have given those seats a higher rating.

Fast, punctual, comfortable and spotlessly clean. Like all of Japan's excellent transport networks, they are of a high standard. I recommend getting the jr pass before leaving to offset the quite high costs, it is also better to book on the busiest routes such as Tokyo-Kyoto.

I took the Nozomi train from Shinagawa to Nagoya. All seats were non-smoking, but there is actually a smoking room every few cars. The exhaled smoke from the passengers sitting next to me returning from the smoking room and those walking down the aisle not only made me uncomfortable, but I also became sick as there was no place to escape in the cramped interior of the car. By providing a smoking room instead of a smoking car, the damage caused by second-hand smoke and third-hand smoke, which until now was mostly limited to smoking cars, will now be spread throughout the train, which is a serious problem. Unless smoking rooms are removed and all cars are made non-smoking like on the Tohoku Shinkansen, I will continue to fly comfortably and safely.

The Shinkansen is very fast and comfortable. Super punctual and easy. Buy the ticket and take the train. It's that easy. The only problem is that it's not easy to find someone who speaks English to guide you, so research everything online before heading out. Oh, no, on the train, you can talk on your cell phone! Things from Japan! Bon voyage!

One of the highlights of our trip to Japan was travelling on the Shinkansen. The best train experience in all of my travels around the world. Super efficient, perfect punctuality, immaculately clean, comfortable, great amenities, great selection of food to purchase on board, plenty of room to store your luggage and always great views from the windows as you speed on through! The only way to travel by land!

First time riding the Shinkansen. Great experience. Quiet and roomy. You can purchase minimal food and drink from a small cart but I highly recommend you bring your own. Announcements are made in both Japanese and English. They said free wifi was available but I didn't know where to get the password. Overall definitely a great experience that I can check off my "must do" list while living in Japan.

On the first day I travelled from Osaka to Nagoya, which usually takes only about an hour. On the particular day of my trip, however, there was a lot of snowfall, which meant that the journey took almost half an hour more, as it slowed the train down quite significantly. Not that this diminished the experience in any way, though. On the contrary, it felt even more exciting!Bullet trains in Japan are extremely efficient and clean, with excellent service and a frequency of services that is quite amazing, so the Tokaido Shinkansen is no exception. I was riding the Hikari.The last time I was travelling this route between Tokyo and Osaka, there were still smoking carriages available, which at the time I found very annoying, because it meant that the smoking carriages were half empty, while the non-smoking carriages tended to be fully booked and felt very crowded. So I was glad to see that now the whole train is non-smoking, and that they now offer small 'smoking rooms' near the bathroom facilities. And ideal solution that serves both smokers and non-smokers.On the second day I travelled from Nagoya to Tokyo. Tip: If you travel eastbound on this route, make sure you get a seat on the left side of the train, as that will allow spectacular views of Mt. Fuji (especially in the winter months, when it's snow-capped). It can be a bit of a challenge to get a photo without any electricity poles or wires in the picture - not least because of the speed of the train -, but you will just have to press the shutter multiple times, and you will be rewarded with magnificent pictures of the highest mountain in Japan.

The train was wonderful, very comfortable and punctual, there are 2 classes, I traveled in first class and the seats are wide and comfortable, they do not provide food, it is advisable to buy what you want before getting on

Shinkansen literally means new trunk line and it is the super fast train that runs upto 200 miles per hour. (320 Km per hr)We took the train from Tokyo to Kyoto for a day trip. It runs so smoothly that you do not realise it is going so fastSuddenly as we travel Mount Fuji comes into view. Mount Fuji is one of Japan's "Three Holy Mountains. It is stunning. Lucky to get a clear view for miles and made this train journey very special.Mount Fuji is an active volcano and was visible with little Fuji too. its height is 3,776.24 m (12,389 ft).The beauty of Mount Fuji is hard to describe - it needs to be experienced, its majestically rises in perfect symmetry wearing the clouds as its umbrella- breathtaking.

Turned up at the booking office in Kyoto, bought an unreserved ticket to Tokyo on the Nozomi, this is the quickest train as it stops the least with its cheapest ticket as no reserved seat which is limited to the first 3 carriages.At the terminal just along the station, It's more like an airplane check in than catching a normal train.  We were on the train in 20 minutes, seats arrangements are 2 on one side and 3 on the other.Luckily we got 2 seats together, loads of leg room (sufficient for us & 2 big flight bags).The journey was swift and smooth, helpfully station announcements were also in English and there was a refreshment cart  although most locals brought on snack boxes they bought in the station.A huge plus was seeing Mt Fuji close up on a clear blue sky day.A great experience and way to travel in Japan.
Great way to travel from Tokyo to Kyoto. Very relaxing but no view of Mt Fuji today. Better luck next time.

Took the JR bullet train from Tokyo to Kyoto  (get your JR pass!) and I can't stop taking about how lovely the experience was. We really don't do train travel well here in the US and Japan trains are the best! Clean, efficient, on time; they have it all. It was about 2.5 hours from Tokyo to Kyoto and you can get a reserved seat. When  you get on the platform, there are signs that tell you where to stand based on your car #. People queue up in an orderly fashion and board the train based on where they are seated. But be warned, they are super efficient and on time so you only have a few moments to board or get off the train.

I traveled around Japan using these trains and they are easy to take, clean, comfortable. The only thing is that it is better to book them in advance to be sure of having a seat: booking does not involve additional costs compared to the ticket or jr pass (which I obviously recommend because the tickets are quite expensive). Track directions are alternated in Japanese and Latin script on the signs. To first see where the platform is, you can start by looking for the timetable on the boards: the trains are punctual to the point of breaking the second, and this allows you to identify your Shinkansen even if the Japanese writing still appears. Really 10+ also for the extreme cleanliness of the bathrooms
I use it frequently for business and private purposes. If the weather is nice this time of year, you can see Mt. Fuji beautifully from the train window and feel happy. (Window seat E is recommended)

The regular car seats three people, with seats A and B on the sea side and CDE seats on the mountain side. Reservations are starting to fill up starting from seat A, which seats two people, but if you want to see Mt. Fuji, seat E is the place to go. Also, the middle D seat for three people is unpopular, so if you're traveling alone, there's a good chance that the seat next to you will be empty. The green car seats both the sea side and the mountain side, so the A seat by the sea side window and the D seat by the mountain side are booked out at the same rate. For your reference when choosing your seat.
Use the Tokaido Shinkansen from Tokyo to Nagoya. I always use EX-IC, so ticket reservations are easy. It's great that you can move on time.
Three consecutive years having my Japan Rail pass travelling anywhere I want in from North to South in Japan.  Highly recommended to travelers, the JR pass is a MUST have when you are in Japan!

Trains are a cult in Japan and now I know why, traveling on a shinkansen is an experience that really gives you a taste of Japanese culture to be precise. Given the comfort on board and the speed of the train, it is impressive how the times are respected to the second. If you are lucky enough to take the train from the terminus, go to the platform at least twenty minutes before departure, wait for the train to arrive and observe the whole complex ritual of reversing the seats and cleaning the train.

We found the trains super efficient but had to ask many people to make sure we if the right platforms it was a bit hard to know what platform you were on if your train was more than an hour away . One little tip is to be quick to get on the train . I was helping a lady get off with her stroller at Matsumoto station and the doors shut and I couldn't get on the train . It was easy to catch the next one but annoying at the time as I was helping a local Japanese lady as no one else did and I thought the least the station master could do was wait for 15 seconds but the Japanese are so efficient they wait for no one.

You really need to experience the fastest train in Japan. The experience is really stunning and really helps you a lot when you need to change city fast or exploring other city while your hotel is in the other one.This is really a game changer for traveler.

It was cheaper than a plane and almost as fast. They sell food everywhere. I would recommend you guys book in advance. We went from Tokyo to Hakodate in under 4 hours. It was very safe and barely felt the train. And seeing the countryside is a very nice change compared to the bright lights off Tokyo metro. Highly recommended!
I used it on my way home on New Year's Day. Since it was the end of the year, it was crowded. When departing from Tokyo, Mt. Fuji can be clearly seen on the right hand side.

*Yes Tohoku/Hokuriku/Hokkaido and Akita Shinkansen use more luxury vehicles, but N700A uses on Tokaido shinkansen still rides better than ICE and TGV and certainly anything in UK, not to mention comfortable*Yes , Tohoku and Akita Shinkansen lines are more scenic , Tokaido Shinkansen go right through world heritage listed heart of Kyoto and foot of the Mt Fuji *Fare are cheaper than airlines, even better of you have Japan Railpass/JR Tokai pass/JR West pass*And trains are frequent, reliable, unlike domestic airlines..!* Service are the best in the world, nothing like lousy domestic airlines...highly recommended

We purchased a seven day rail pass for our trip to Japan and it has been worth every penny spent.  If you are headed to Japan you will be well aware that it is a very expensive country to visit.  The use of a JR rail pass will help you significantly cut down your travel costs between cities and in some cities.  The pass can be used on all JR tracks which means that you can use them on some of the tracks within larger cities like Tokyo, Osaka and Kyoto.  If you arrange for your lodging near a JR station, then your movements will be easier and cheaper.  The Shinkansen trains run frequently and are very easy to book in any station with a JR ticket office.  In the larger stations they will have two counters, one for current day travel and one for future travel and they are well signed so they are easy to find.  The trains run frequently in between cities and you can either reserve a seat or take your chances with one of the non reserved cars.  We tended to use the reserved cars as it made our planning a bit easier but also took non reserved as well when we did day trips.  The cars are spacious and comfortable but luggage can be a bit if a challenge.  There are racks overhead for your bags but if you are using large bags, they can be hard to get up and there are no designated spaces for luggage on the trains.  If you do decide to purchase the rail pass you need to do so before your trip as I don't believe that you can do it once in country.  You will get sent a voucher which you exchange for your pass once you are in Japan and this can be done in the airports or at the larger stations.  You will want to be careful though on your dates so that you don't  run out of time.  There are two kinds of passes, the regular and the green passes which are for the first class cars.  We were more than happy with the regular passes as the cars are quite comfortable so were quite happy we did not spend the extra money on the green pass.  If you are headed to Japan, this is the only way to travel.  The trains are fast, on time and incredibly convenient.

Taking the Shinkansen is such a hassle free experience. They are regular, on time, clean and comfortable. Recently we spent 10 days in Japan and took nearly a dozen trips on the Shinkansen and every one of them was pleasurable. The signs are mostly in English and if you are traveling with a JR pass its so easy even a beginner can do it. Station staff are also very helpful.....I would totally recommend it! You can choose between reserved and non reserved seating depending on your preference and the length of your journey and watch the beautiful Japanese countryside speed by!
One of the best trains I have ridden in terms of cleanliness, speed, and punctuality in the second. It is best to choose first class seats, which are quiet and provide chairs unlike regular class.

The fastest and most punctual travel by train anywhere in the world. Precise leaving and arrival times (oftentimes in Europe, I'm not totally rushing to catch a train, since there is a good chance that it will have been delayed in leaving). Great customer service too, with white gloved guards bowing whenever they leave a carriage (almost all Japanese have such great manners, it really is something to aspire to). The trains are comfortable in standard class, and all seats sit frontwards (they're actually spun 180 degrees to face the right way on the return journey). Lots of leg room. The two things that I was surprised by were - the rolling stock is actually quite old (but like so many things in Japan, because it's of good quality and well maintained, it lasts) and there is no wifi. Be great if Shinkansen could exist on the London Paddington to Bath line...

We took the Bullet train Nozomi (fastest) from Kyoto to Tokyo.  It's been a while since I haven't ridden a Shinkansen.  Just to add to the excellent trip, we got to be in a Green car (first class).  The seat arrangement is 2 and 2 (the other cars have 2 and 3, little narrower seats) and the car has Oshibori (wet towel) service. I was determined to see my home town area from the train windows.  Alas, when I woke up from my unintended doze off (perhaps due to the jet lag), the train was already in the next prefecture, fast approaching Nagoya (mid point)!  The whole trip took about 2 hours and 20 minutes.  From one city center to another city center, it saves your valuable time.  It's convenient, comfortable, and, above all, very fast!  An excellent way to travel Japan.
Perhaps not the cheapest, but one of the fastest ways to get from Tokyo to Kyoto. At the same time, it’s comfortable and strictly on schedule!

Most of my recent business trips have been to western Japan, and even if I'm going east, I've been flying a lot, so I took the Shinkansen for the first time in a while. Since our destination was within Shizuoka Prefecture, I was looking forward to seeing Mt. Fuji from the train window, but unfortunately we couldn't see it at all due to the bad weather.

I was able to ride the bullet train on the way back from my tour to Mount Fuji.The train rides really smooth although it travels at speeds of over 300 kms an hour.  You can even buy food on the train or buy your own at the station and eat on board.  I also got to take the train from Tokyo to Osaka which as about 2.5 hours.  It is a reasonable price for tickets too, but I also found discount tickets on japanican.com.  I think they were 20% discount for Tokyo to Osaka return.  You can collect your ticket at Tokyo station either beforehand or day of.  I had a voucher, but the tour desk wasn't open till 10 am so I ended up leaving closer to noon since they had to find a train leaving that morning that was still available to Osaka.  Unreserved seats are in the first few cars of the train.  They do check to make certain you have a ticket for the right seating location about halfway through the ride.  They moved someone sitting next to me because they were in the wrong car.   So beware.  There is vending machines and bathrooms on board too for your convenience too.
Clean, spacious, on time. Purchase your passes abroad or at the Shinkansen station. Great ride from Kyoto to Odawara!

We booked the Nozumi from Tokyo to Kyoto. It got us bang on time within 2 hrs 20mins.Tip: don't buy JR pass unless you are doing a round trip back to Tokyo. Reserve early and get the seats on the right side to see the view of Mount Fuji.

We can't speak highly enough of the JR Shinkansen system of Japan. On all our journeys in our recent five week trip to Japan, all the trains were clean, well-serviced, punctual; with the staff being courteous and helpful. The JR rail passes are a credit to the company and we encourage all visitors to Japan to investigate them. On one occasion, I left my 'good' hat hanging on the peg provided and alighted without it. On realising, we went immediately to the Lost and Found section at Kyoto where they quickly took details and phoned the train to secure its return. Long story short, it was returned to our hotel two days later in good order. We were very impressed. I wish our public transport system operated as efficiently.

This is a Japanese railway that can be proud to the world. I don't think it can be compared to the railroads in our neighbors' countries where they imitate people. Even though they look the same, the vehicles, seats, ride comfort, speed, durability, and other technologies are all excellent. In fact, you can tell by comparing the rides.

Quite simply, the Bullet Trains are the best trains we have ever been on.  As well as their impressive speed, we found them to be very comfortable and easy to use.  New visitors to Japan may be daunted about using them, but we found that Tokyo and Kyoto stations were easy to navigate and the staff were all happy to help.  Signs are in English as well as Japanese and the location of each carriage is clearly marked on the platforms.  We watched the turnaround of the train at Tokyo and it was fascinating to see an army of cleaners prepare the train and turn the seats around so that they face forwards on each trip.  Once on board there is plenty of space, numerous spotlessly clean toilets and a very frequent trolley service.The smartness of all of the railway staff and their pride in this railway that is arguably the best in the world was plain to see.

So smooth! We travelled from Tokyo station to Shin-Osaka station. The trip took exactly 2h 33m.We arranged tickets through our travel agent and they arrived at our hotel 2 days before we departed but you can buy them at the station too. Most of the information you need is printed on the ticket - name of the train, departure time, arrival time, carriage, seat number.When you arrive at the station you just need to check which platform to go to - even if you don't read Japanese, just look for the train name in English. If in doubt the staff at the gates will point you to the correct platform. Arrive about 15-20 minutes before the departure time to give you plenty of time to find the platform and then walk to the appropriate gate for your carriage - it's a long platform. We got onto the platform around the spot for carriage 16 and had to walk down to the gate for carriage 8 with 3 suitcases. Thankfully we were early and did not have to dodge other commuters to get to our gate.Once you find your gate, form a line behind anyone else waiting at your gate. Don't cut the queue. Tokyo station is the end/start of the line so cleaners will need to freshen up the carriage before you board.After the cleaners leave, board the train and find your seat. Small bags should fit over your seat. If you have large suitcases you can ask a member of staff where to put it. Remember to turn your mobile phones to silent. Then sit back and get comfy. There is supposed to be wifi on the train but we couldn't figure it out. Trolleys of refreshments (coffee, coke, beer, sandwiches, nuts, etc) will pass by occasionally. They take cash and cards.The whole thing was so easy and comfortable. I think we will be shinkansen-ing all over Japan on future trips.

I visited Japan with my family with 3 kids and 4 large luggages. It's a nightmare traveling on Shinkansen this way. To be fair, I think that it's an efficient and cost-saving way if I'm traveling alone with a backpack or a business travel with a cabin luggage. The door is small and walkway narrow and difficult to navigate around. The train is very punctual which makes it stressful to get up and down the train with kids and a few large luggages. The Japanese, I realized, were very particular about their allotted space. There was a man seated besides me who even refused to close up his legs slightly for me to turn my luggage, in my attempt to free up more space. I find this encounter very strange.My advice, for family traveling with kids, take the internal flights.

I rode the Tokaido Shinkansen between Nagoya and Osaka. You can get from Tokyo to Osaka by train and it stops at all the big stations such as Yokohama, Nagoya and Kyoto. The price of the ticket is determined by the distance, for me it was 5380 Yen, so this is not the cheapest end. However, the ride is fast, comfortable and punctual in the Japanese style. Around 3,000 yen would have gotten by by taking the bus. I didn't think it was worth the effort.

Il n’y a pas de meilleure façon de juger les trains rapides japonais que d’établir une comparaison avec les TGV français que nous connaissons bien.Ce n’est pas la première fois que je dois me rendre à l’aéroport de Roissy CDG.Chaque fois c’est le même désagrément : Il n’y a pas de place pour les valises !Depuis des années, la SNCF n’a toujours pas compris que les personnes prenant l’avion ont besoin d’un volume de racks à bagages suffisant dans ce train desservant un aéroport.J’ai connu (presque à chaque fois) des empilements anarchiques de valises dans le sas de l’entrée avec l’impossibilité de gagner ma place réservée.Réflexion du contrôleur, alors que j’étais assis coincé sur un genre de strapontin dans le sas rempli de passagers et de bagages: « Vous avez une place réservée, pourquoi vous ne l’occupez pas ? ». Réponse : « Je fais comment pour m’y rendre, la circulation est bloquée de partout ? »Revenant (pour la seconde fois) du Japon où j’ai utilisé le Japan Rail Pass pendant 2 semaines pour parcourir le pays du sud au nord) je peux témoigner que les trains rapides Shinkansen sont confortables, bien insonorisés, toujours à l’heure, sans mauvaises surprises de grèves à répétition, avec de l’espace et un service à bord (2e classe) absolument impeccable.Quant aux toilettes et lavabos, ils sont plus nombreux plus modernes et mieux dimensionnés.En comparaison, on peut juger que notre SNCF est bien médiocre.L’envoi en stage des cadres de la SNCF chez leurs collègues japonais permettrait de leur ouvrir les yeux et de s’inspirer de ce qui se fait de mieux en matière de transport par rail.Je voyais récemment dans la presse qu’en Normandie, à cause des feuilles mortes, les trains de Paris – Granville partent en retard ou en avance et qu’ils sont parfois remplacés par des cars. On croit rêver. Il y a aussi la chute des feuilles des arbres au Japon, mais leurs trains ne patinent pas et sont d'une ponctualité qui émerveille.On comprend que les usagers français soient excédés.Pour en revenir aux Shinkansens  japonais, jugez de leur disposition et de l’espace à bord :D’un côté une rangée de 3 fauteuils ; de l’autre une rangée de 2 fauteuils et entre les deux une large allée avec un constant service de snacks, et ekiben (bento ferroviaire) boissons chaudes et froides par du personnel d’une courtoisie exceptionnelle. On dispose évidemment d'une tablette et d'un porte gobelet. En prime, des prises permettent d'alimenter ordinateur ou smartphone et le wi-fi fonctionne parfaitement.... et il y a de la place pour mettre ses valises !Lorsqu’un contrôleur ou une personne du service de restauration entre dans un wagon, il commence par saluer (en s’inclinant) l’ensemble des passagers et il fait de même (en se retournant) quand il quitte le wagon.Les portes séparant les wagons s’ouvrent d’un effleurement de la main et n’ont pas la fâcheuse habitude de se refermer prématurément.Autre innovation : chaque rangée de fauteuils ( 3 et 2) comporte une pédale permettant de déverrouiller la base pour disposer les assises dans le sens de la marche ou inversement. La manœuvre ne demande aucun effort ; un enfant pouvant retourner seul les rangées.Nous étions une famille de 3 adultes à voyager avec 3 enfants. Pour les longs trajets, nous pouvions choisir de nous faire face pour jouer aux cartes, ou converser par exemple.Quant aux trains (monorail pour l’aéroport de Tokyo Haneda) qui vont vers les aéroports de grands espaces à bagages sont aménagés et la circulation est aisée.Le niveau des quais est parfaitement plan avec le seuil de la porte des trains et l'interstice entre quai et wagon est réduit pour la sécurité.Les valises passent sans difficulté du quai au plancher du wagon, alors que dans les wagons surbaissés ( à étage) de la SNCF il faut passer par des marches qui descendent. Enfin le couloir, plus large qu’à bord des trains français, fait que l’on ne heurte pas les accoudoirs des sièges en passant avec sa valise.La signalétique au sol pour les différents trains est parfaite et la politesse légendaire des japonais fait que descendre et monter se fait sans anarchie, même aux heures d'affluence.Oui les japonais sont « les seigneurs du rail ». Ils ont tout à nous apprendre.A ce sujet je lisais dans le guide de Claude Leblanc : « Le Japon vu du train » ceci (page 59): « en 50 années d’exploitation le Shinkansen n’a jamais connu d’accident mortel » et encore ceci (page 62): « Lors du tremblement de terre-tsunami du 11 mars 2011, aucun des trains n’est sorti de ses rails avec des passagers à bord malgré la violence extrême de la secousse. Il faut dire que des progrès considérables ont été réalisés par les ingénieurs nippons. Même les trains à grande vitesse qui circulaient au moment du séisme ont réussi à s’arrêter sans encombre. … La seule fois où un Shinkansen a déraillé lors d’un séisme, ce fut en 2004 lors du tremblement de terre qui a secoué la région de Nigata à 350 kilomètres au nord de Tokyo, mais sans faire de victimes."Chapeau bas, Mesdames Messieurs les cheminots japonais. Nos « cocoricos » chauvins à propos de nos TGV n’impressionnent que ceux qui n’ont jamais mis les pieds au Japon ni pris le Shinkansen.Quand on connait le Japon et son peuple, on revient plus humble en France.

So speedy and roomy. Travelled from Tokyo to Kyoto and back. If you want views of Mt. Fuji you need to sit on the right hand side of the train leaving Tokyo and left hand returning to Tokyo. Unfortunately, weather often precludes a view. However, scenery is interesting as you pass through small cities, towns and rural areas. I took a bento box onboard but there is a snack trolley. For smokers there are smoking rooms (one in carriage 15 for example). Toilets are clean but sometimes a wait as you get close to stops.
Quite a European station with duplicating information in English. Lots of coffee shops and kiosks. Simple and clear navigation

In January of this year, when I traveled to Kansai, I rode for the first time in about 30 years. I often ride the Tohoku Shinkansen, Hokuriku Shinkansen, and Joetsu Shinkansen. Compared to these, there are many things to see from the train window, such as Mt. Fuji, the emerald-colored Lake Hamana, and Kyoto's Toji Temple. If you ride regularly, you're used to it and probably don't care about it anymore, but if you ride it occasionally, you'll find it interesting.

A vehicle for long journeys, comfortable and fast. A must do if you come to Japan. It is better to get the Japan Rail Pass, expensive if you use it little, but very convenient if you make a lot of trips, it lasts a week.

Although it has become quite spacious, the green cars are not as spacious compared to other railways around the world. Considering the number of guests, we would like to have a compartment or a space where meetings can be held. JR Kyushu may have already done this.

Wow- these go fast although when you are travelling on one it is very comfortable and troublefree. We had three separate journeys Osaka to Kyoto, Kyoto to Tokyo and Mt Fuji back to Tokyo. All in time all the way.It is only when you see one pass you while you are in the platform that you realise how fast these are.On board they are comfortable with plenty of leg room. Passengers all treat the train with respect (as they do everything else in Japan) which means it works like clockwork.A must as you travel around Japan

The Japanese have got their public transport sorted. Clean, efficient, economical and reliable. The topper is that the shinkansen trains are also pretty cool.  All the things Australian public transport is not. Maybe one day.

I'm not even that big of a train buff, but thoroughly loved going on the Shinkansen for an hour or so. There's something so very japenese about careening through the countryside at 270 mph, enjoying the views and knowing that you're traveling on what is essentially a commuter train. Gotta love it -- and it's not all that expensive either. Treat yourself to a trip to Mt Fuji!

These trains are amazing. If you have a rail pass you can cruise the country in luxury at up to 300kph. Prompt service. Heaps of legroom even for tall westerners and a great view of the countryside. The bonus is they drop you in the centre of town so there is no hassle with airport transfers.
These are very clean, efficient and very fast, they are just brilliant. The U.K. could really learn from the bullet train.

Wow......when you talk about being on time.....this is the Japanese railway system and the BULLET TRAIN. Efficient, clean and prompt , it was a great way to travel and see Japan.The JR pass ( please ensure you purchase it outside Japan as it is not available in Japan and it will cost you a fortune to travel without it!!) was excellent and cost effective.I loved it!! Hopefully, other cities in the world can learn from excellent and prompt scheduling and polite staff to guide you.

It was a very interesting trip for us. It was a very outstanding experience for us when we joined the domestic railway. We were able to rebook a comfortable, accurate, seat ticket on the train. And we crossed half of Japan in a few hours. :)To see Fuji, take a seat on the right side of the Tokyo - Osaka line! :)If you want to travel at a good price, buy the JR pass from home in advance!!!

We travelled from Tokyo to Osaka and return by what the Japanese call the Shinkansen and most visitors call the Bullet Train. Trains run very frequently. Just remember, trains run from Shin-Osaka station, which is on the outskirts of the city. Get the subway to the station, but allow time for misdirection. The Shinkansen runs at up to 320 km an hour. The Tokyo-Osaka line is only one section of the Shinkansen network. Btw, you must buy your Japan Rail Pass outside of Japan, you would be crazy to come to Japan without one. You can ride on many Japan Rail lines in addition to the Shinkansen with your Pass.

We travelled from Tokyo to Kyoto on the nozomi shinkansen and really enjoyed the experience. It cost 26,180 yen for a return journey which is a bit pricey but it was well worth the money. As the journey started at tokyo there was no need to reserve a seat. To get a seat you want I advise that you get a train that actually starts from tokyo as the ones that are passing through can be busy. Once you board one of the carriages 1-3 try to sit on the right side as you may get a good view of Mt fuji depending on the weather. They have a food a drinks trolley which offers a good choice of hot and cold drinks and sandwiches. I personally bought a bento  box from the station which is actually a full meal on a box. Finally a quick word about the train. It's incredibly clean and the staff are incredibly efficient as you would expect in japan. Yes it's expensive to use but it took 2 hours 18 minutes so it was worth it

I took the Shinkansen from Hamamatsu Station for the first time. Hikari only stops once per hour, and Kodama only stops twice per hour. I rode on the way back to Tokyo, so I timed it to coincide with the light. There are quite a few people boarding from Hamamatsu, so I thought it would be a good idea to go to the platform early and wait in line for non-reserved seats.

Traveling on the Shinkansen is a real experience: the trains are almost never late, the carriages are very clean, the seats are comfortable and drinks and snacks are sold during the journey. And all of this at very high speed.

Although it may not be easy for general travelers who do not use the JR Pass, it is the fastest train connecting Tokyo and Osaka. Although the seats are arranged in a 2+3 configuration, it feels more spacious and comfortable than the KTX.

This bullet train is far better than flying between cities. And more comfortable. We had two large suitcases, which the overhead shelves accommodated well. The leg space and reclining seat was welcome. Seats can be heated and phones charged. We enjoyed the scenery, the clean bathroom and the friendly staff. We are planning to depart for Tokyo shortly; looking forward to it.

Fastest transportation for Osaka-Kyoto-Tokyo. We had the opportunity to try Nozomi from Kyoto-Osaka. We thought this train departed every hour or even every few hours. However, it turns out that the departure schedule can be 7-9 times an hour, especially during peak hours in the morning and afternoon. This means that every 5-10 minutes there is a departure. What's more, if we choose a non-reserved ticket (a ticket without a seat number), then we can use the ticket at any time in the day (but only used once). If the ticket has a seat number, then the time, carriage and seat number are specified. Arriving at Tokyo station, we can still use the Shinkansen ticket to ride the local train once. When we exit through the automatic door, when we insert the ticket, the ticket doesn't come out again. Comfort on the train is also very good. It doesn't feel like we are traveling on a train at speeds above 200km/hour. You only feel the difference when you walk on the train. However, if you just sit in a train seat, it doesn't seem like it's any different from riding a regular train.

We were a little disappointed not to find any luggage racks by the entrance, meaning we had to carry heavy and awkward bags down the narrow aisles to our seats. However the amount of seat space was extremely generous, meaning you can easily fit a couple of big cases between you and the back of the seat in front. Ticket inspectors, and food vendors walked by a few times, each bowing as they entered the carriage and greeting the passengers. The trains were exceptionally clean and the trip was fantastically quick. Pity you can't purchase tickets online.

We head to Tokyo Station to take the 10:36 a.m. Shinkansen to Utsunomiya. For this type of train, you can reserve your seat in advance, or enter unreserved carriages. In this case the first come, first served rule prevails. We place ourselves in line according to the markings indicated on the platform, so that there is no jostling. The train arrives a little before departure time, and after the passengers disembark, agents turn the seats so that they all face the direction of travel. Cleaning is also carried out before the next passengers, including us, can board. So we move forward in line, everyone enters the car one by one. The cleanliness and comfort of the train are remarkable...! Finally, the Shinkansen leaves right on time, we never noticed a single minute of delay!

We took the Shinkansen from Tokyo to Osaka and it was amazing.  The speed does not seem anywhere as quick as you are actually travelling with plenty of time to look at the passing scenery.  If you get a bit peckish then the trolley service, although a little expensive is great and has everything from sandwiches to chocolate.  We had sandwiches and they were extremely fresh, nothing to complain about.  Would certainly use this form of transport again.

We took the Tokaido from Osaka to Kyoto as I wanted to re experience my last trip from 1985.We were in the last two carriages as these are not booked seats. We had to sit seperately but the seats are spacious with plenty of leg room.Snack cart came through as we went along however it is quick and it only took 15 minutes to travel the distance.A really quick comfortable trip however not cheap. The express regional trains are fast but no where near this speed but cheaper.Worth the price if travelling longer distances.

I used a package tour on my trip to Nagoya.I enjoyed the view from the train window on the Kodama train.I boarded the train from Shin-Yokohama Station, so it was less crowded than Tokyo Station, and it was a comfortable 700 series train with an outlet.

The bullet train is without a doubt an integral part of visiting Japan. Whizzing through Japan on the Shinkansen at a speed close to 300km/h is a nice experience and a great way to travel. However. I feel the need to write about the JR Pass as I have seen a lot of confusion about the pass and tons of publicity and ads for it that complicate the decision process.The most important point to remember is that although you cannot buy the JR Pass (physically) in Japan. You can buy it online and get it delivered to an address in Japan.I have ordered mine when I was in Japan through a website in the UK and I got the voucher delivered to my hotel in 2 days. Then went and changed the voucher for the actual travel card at a ticketing station. The travel card cannot be used So you can get the pass voucher delivered to your hotel in Japan without a problem. However think carefully if you really need it and don't rush the decision. Here are few pointers that I hope will help. And don't get caught by all the marketing buzz that's on the Internet. If you don't get it today it is not the end of the world. You will live and you will survive without it. Trust me. In Japan there is a solution for everything. Firstly not all trains are JR trains hence there are many services were the JR pass is not acceptable. So check where you want to go first and then decide. The Metro in Tokyo is not part is the service so JR pass will not give you access to the metro. The Portliner in Kobe isn't part of it either and the list goes on and on. So do check what services you'll be using. Ideally if you are going from OSAKA to TOKYO and back on the JR network (for example) each leg will cost around Y14500 (Roughly USD130) or Y29,000 Return (USD 260). The 7 days JR rail pass for the standard class is Y29,110). If you will be traveling on the JR networks for couple more destinations then getting the Pass is a good idea. I personally wouldn't getting just for this trip alone. As I said ealier If you don't get the pass it is not the end of the world you can always buy the tickets from the ticket office the rates are similar to the prices of TGV in France and other fast trains in Europe. Or do what I have done since I was staying 3 days in Kobe. I ordered the voucher online whilst I was in Kobe and got it delivered to my hotel. Then went and exchanged it at the JR ticket office. Most ticket offices are item till 2300 and more. If you are in Japan only for a week and mostly staying in one city. Do yourself a favour and check any trips you plan on doing on Google Map. It will show you the public transport options as well as the fares. And then make your decision accordingly. It will probably be not worth buying it for a short period if you are not using JR often. And remember that many trains are not part of the JR network so you cannot use your pass on these anyway. Local transport costs is not expensive in Japan.One more thing JR doesn't automatically mean that the train is a bullet train (Shinkansen). In Japan there are 6 different bullet trains I believe. Yet there are many trains on many routes on the JR network that aren't even close to the bullet train. So most of the travel for shorter distances will be on normal trains and the fares are very cheap anyway.Bullets will only run on the longer legs. And the JR pass will not give you access to the fastest of the bullet train (Nozomi). You will be able to use the other Shinkansens but not the Nozomi trains. Another reason to check you itinerary before taking the decision. The normal train ticket cost is cheap. Also note that to reserve your seat on the shinkansen you need to be present in person at the ticket office and reserve your seat prior to departure. You cannot reserve you seat online. There is no dedicated luggage storage space on the bullet trains. You need to keep your luggage either in front of you which won't give you much leg room. Or keep it in a very limited space behind the last seats in the carriage. Which will probably fit 6 medium size bags in total (Check the attached photos). Also remember that the JR passes cannot be used on the automatic gates. So you need to find a station officer and present your pass (es) to the him/her and he/she will let you through on the way in to and out of the station. This could be tricky in larger cities such as Tokyo where many large stations have only Automatic Gates on most of the side/smaller Entrances and the station officers are only available in the main entrance.Few times I showed up at smaller station entrances and could not find an officer so couldn't use the Pass and I had to buy a cheap ticket (any one) to get in. And then show my pass on the way out. The local tickets are cheap. But this defeats the purpose.If you do your homework and decide to get the Pass you can purchase the the Standard Pass or the Green Pass which is equivalent to Business class at a roughly ¥10,000 extra (for the 7 days pass).I personally have opted for this as the carriage  is less crowded, the seats are roomier and more comfy. (Check the photo of the Green Carriage)It's a personal choice if your budget permits. But it won't get you to your destination any faster :)Hope this information is helpful.
This is easily the best train service I have ever been on. Fast, efficient and brilliantly priced. It will make your stay in Japan very convenient.

We had been ticketed to Tokyo JR with a switch to the Narita Express on our second last day in Japan.  Our Kyoto guide, Mr. Hiroshi Tsuyama, explained that the switch in Tokyo would be complicated by the size of the station and the difficulty of finding the Narita Express in the time available.  He had us re-ticketed to Shinagawa, one station prior to Tokyo JR, and to catch the Narita train there.  The station at Shinagawa is much smaller and easier to maneuver.  It worked like a charm and we are indebted to him from saving us from a costly missed connection.  This was the last Narita train of the day.The green cars on this line are very clean and comfortable, and not crowded at all.  There is ample overhead space for carry-ons, so this is not a problem on any green car train.  Use of the Japan Rail Pass got us everywhere we wanted to go in clean comfort using the green cars.

Do not hesitate to take a train in Tokyo Station and do not fear SHINKANSEN, is TOP! People are very friendly and willing to help and you get extra information by reading the signage.You may be surprised by seeing a human face from the inside of a ticket machine offering support.That happened to our family while we were facing some challenges while we tried to buy our tickets to Nagano. We laugh and my kids couldn't stop!  Seats are comfortable and if you are traveling with kids or a group of friends you may find a way of moving seats in order to face them properly. By the way ... everything is super clean and the Train cleaning team appears in a line once is finished wishing you a safe trip ! so beautiful ! You need to try!

During a recent vacation to Japan our group had the pleasure of riding the "Shin" several times and to many different locations during a two week period. What can I say that hasn't already been said?  The Shin are very sleek in appearance, very clean, smooth,quiet, and of course fast. We clocked one of our trips at 175 mph. What I can add are some tips. First of all as many have said you need to purchase your JR Rail tickets before your arrival. Once you arrive at your point of entry make sure the Japan customs agent places a landing permission sticker in your passport to prove you are a tourist. With this and your rail pass purchase receipt you can proceed to a JR location to get your pass activated.  2.  The trains and Shin in Japan run on time so if you plan on traveling on a certain train it will be there when they say and they won't wait for you. Be early. 3.  During our travels we didn't pay extra for green car passes, we found the reserved seating provided plenty of room both in seating and leg room. You can actually rotate your bank of seats if you want to talk with your friends behind you.  4.  Reserved seats are free you just need to go to a ticket office and make the reservation. Your reserved tickets are only good for the train you reserve for, so once again be on time. 5.  Finally, if you are dragging large luggage we found it best to enter the door near the back of the car that you are riding in. Usually there is enough storage room behind the last row of seats to stow your luggage.  Carry on sized luggage, bags, packs can be stored on a large shelf above your seats.   Many have said the rail passes are expensive, they are, but your passes will allow you to ride many other trains, and buses around Japan, some of the subways in Tokyo, and even the ferries to Miyiajima so they end up being a great value.

Got the train from Kyoto to Tokyo.We had not booked in advance as we checked and were told no need. The trains come so regularly like every 6 mins at the time we were travelling which was morning.Decided to pay the extra and book the green car and so very glad we did. The seats are larger and very comfortable with usb, power sockets , fold down table,reading light and foot rest. The carriage was less than half full. There are plenty of clean toilets and even an enclosed smoking room if needed. There us a very. Regular drink service and also snacks. The train is super clean and is on time to.The SECOND. Don't miss

When traveling to Japan don't forget to get your JR rail pass before you leave for Japan.  While you may think it is expensive, it is the best investment you will make for your trip to Japan, especially if you pay the extra $100 and get the green (business class) pass.  When you get to Japan you exchange it for a 7 or 14 day pass, then you can ride all the JR local trains, buses and ferries, as well as most of the Shinkansens going all over Japan.  We always get the green class pass as you can travel in style with more comfort in a quiet cabin with larger seats, but you can also book normal reserved class.  With a green pass you will be almost guaranteed a seat in the green cabin as it is never full even on booked out trains in ordinary class.  This is the best ticket we have ever bought and it is great value and a must for all tourists.  Go JR their trains are easy to use and FAST, not to mention reliable.

When moving around Tokyo Station, I have to walk such a long distance that I feel like I'm in a monotonous mood. Is this because the Shinkansen exit occupies the first floor or basement of the Yaesu exit? Previously, I used to take round trips, but these days I only take occasional trips and often use local trains, so I'm a bit dissatisfied.

A japanese holiday is not complete if you don't travel by Shinkansen. And if you want to travel extensively while in Japan a JR Pass is a must. We travelled from Tokyo to Kyoto by Hikari Shinkansen and the experience is amazing. You can even take from the railway station in Tokyo lunch boxes (bento) and the drinks can be bought in the train. Stay on the right if you want to see the impressive Mount Fuji. Shinkansen is a symbol for japanese people which have never had an incident. So it's safe, reliable, comfortable and very fast!

We started our journey to the second, after each car had been cleaned by the cleaning staff and the seats had been turned in the direction of travel. The trip was flawless, very pleasant and on time. On the way a lady came by with a food cart. You must have booked the Japan Pass for 1, 2 or 3 weeks of train travel within Japan at least one week before departure and will be exchanged for a “general subscription” on site! The cost for a week is around €260 and decreases with each additional week. The investment is worth it when you consider the high individual costs of the trips. Don't forget to reserve your seats if you don't want to run the risk of not getting a seat!

This line represents the Shinkansen that Japan is proud of. If you want to see Mt. Fuji from the train window, reserve the E seat. The green car seats 2 and 2 people, and the reserved and unreserved seats seat 3 people (ABC) and 2 people (DE). (The seats can rotate, so if you are in a group, you can sit facing each other.) Depending on the stop and speed, there are Nozomi, Hikari, and Kodama. Nozomi is the fastest and has fewer stops. This time, I boarded the Kodama train between Shin-Osaka Station and Gifu-Hashima Station and sat in a reserved seat. Compared to previous vehicles, even the reserved seats are more spacious. Please note that no one other than the person occupying a reserved seat in the green car is allowed to stand in the aisle of the green car. However, if the reserved seats are full, people who only have non-reserved seat tickets will be in the aisle. (Reserved seats mean that only the seats are reserved.) Especially during Golden Week, Obon, and New Year's holidays, the aisles are full of people with non-reserved seats, which is annoying. (There isn't that much of a difference, so you can just buy a reserved seat ticket, but there are a lot of people who are stingy with it.) We recommend making reservations early, especially during busy periods.
Today taking family who came from Rio to visit Japan today going to Kyoto, Osaka and Nara. Very good shinkansen train.

As part of a package from Tokyo to Osaka (roundtrip), it was a good deal because otherwise, the Bullet Train can be expensive for backpackers. Having said that, it's quite the experience - like riding an airplane on the ground! Great service, great efficiency time-wise, and of course, the speed is pretty amazing.
Riding the Shinkansen is really one of the must do items.  Particularly exciting for the kids when the bullet train passes other trains.
This is absolutely the very best. Always on-time and always very comfortable. Expensive but a real bargain with the JR Pass. 5 trips in 14 days this year cannot get better.
A visit to Japan would not be complete without a ride on the bullet train. A maximum speed of 320km/h a road trip would have taken 90 minutes, by bullet train 23 minutes !!

It's not the bullet train but it goes very fast and is very precise! They are super monitored by dedicated personnel on the platform! You must book at least 24 hours in advance to find a place because it is only with reserved seats. Simple to take.

We travelled from Tokyo to Kyoto and back in a day. The bullet train is so easy, we left from Tokyo station and two and three quarter hours later stepped out in the middle of Kyoto. We were in standard class but allocated our seats a couple of days prior, which turned out to be smart because on that Friday it was busy up and back.  The seats are reasonably comfy with decent leg room. The overhead baggage shelf is modest and if you have big cases you may have to put them in front of your legs. We sat in seats on the right side of the train down and the left side back in order to have a view of Mount Fuji but sadly it was shrouded in cloud. On the way home we discovered you can save about 20 minutes travel time to Shinjuku or the surrounding suburbs on the Yamanote line by hopping off the train one stop before Tokyo station (don't recall the name sorry)

Traveled to Kyoto on one of these stunning trains. Made booking so got tickets with carriage and seat allocation. Station was well signed platform etc. In fact you knew where to stand exactly ( British railways please note!)it was on time both departure and arrival ( on board announcement in English as well) overall impressive.
Japan's proud Shinkansen. Fast, comfortable and safe. It's expensive so I can only ride it for business, but my child loves Shinkansen so I'd like to give him a ride someday.

If you have an Express Card and a smartphone that accepts Mobile Suica, it's convenient because you can do everything from making reservations to buying tickets on your smartphone. The price will also be lower.

These bullet trains are amazingly fast! They're a quick (and economical with JR pass) way to travel between cities in Japan. Luggage is no problem and the staff are polite and efficient. On one journey I asked the conductor when we might see Mt Fuji- she pulled out a laminated timetable and showed me the exact time we could see the mountain! Most we travelled on had charging points, so we were able to recharge our devices. Every single Shinkansen we caught ran on time- to the minute!! They are also quite frequent. We reserved our seats when we were moving our luggage around, so that we were guaranteed seats. I would also recommend staying at accommodation close to the JR stations, as it's even easier to transport your luggage.

Japan's Shinkansen is famous for its punctuality, speed and safety. This Tokaido Shinkansen is often used by office workers and people traveling for business. When I took the non-reserved seat back to Tokyo in the evening, I encountered a group of office workers returning from a business trip. A group of people were drinking in the carriage, and they became excited and noisy. They used the Shinkansen carriage as a mobile izakaya, and they were unable to have a good rest.

If you can afford the difference, upgrade to green passes. Trains are very fast and very smooth and very punctual!Green cars add that bit extra seat comfort and leg room. In order to guarantee your seat, reserve your seat at a JR office.

I used it for sightseeing. The seats on the Shinkansen are wider than those on airplanes, and I was able to spend a comfortable time traveling with less shaking. One of the great pleasures of traveling by train is riding the Shinkansen and leisurely eating delicious ekiben while watching the scenery flow by.

I live in the Netherlands and our public transport often experiences delays. So it really is true in Japan the train can leave on time. This form of transport is really perfect. Good seat, nice clean compartment, nice train staff and above all on time. Highly recommended to travel through Japan by train.

I got on train number: Hikari superexpress 470 at 1.40pm on 22/9/16 with departure from Shin-Osaka and arrival scheduled for 4.40pm (3 hours of travel for 419 km) with stops in Kyoto, Nagoya, Hamamatsu, Shizuoka, Mishima, Shin Yokohama, Shinagawa and Tokyo. The comfortable seats, the immaculate train, every now and then the train attendant appears, dressed in beige, he enters carriage 13 (almost all Western passengers) bows and says hello. My gaze follows him to the other side before moving on to the next carriage he turns and bows. But the food and drink attendant who passes by every now and then with his trolley does the same thing. The toilets are very clean, you can't smoke, only in a couple of dedicated carriages. Train very punctual! What can I say... A dream!

The Shinkansen ("Bullet Train") is really a small experience in itself. As mentioned in some other travel guides, the travelers really celebrate the ride. With food, drinks and desserts that they bring with them. The seats are ALWAYS facing forward, there are none that are facing backwards. The seats can be rotated by the staff using a small switch. There are no rubbish bins, passengers simply take their rubbish with them. The whole coexistence in the city is based on this, including on the train. With the obligatory seat reservation - and free for holders of the Japan Rail Pass - there are seats A, B, C on the left side and seats D, E on the right side. So if you're traveling with two people, it's best to book the right side and have a double seat. The armrests there can also be raised. On the journey there is also a small snack cart that passed by twice and from which you can buy coffee/tea and snacks. The constantly patrolling conductor bows every time before entering and leaving the carriage, a show of respect for the passengers.

The Shinkansen is comfortable no matter when you ride it. The Tokaido Shinkansen has two and three rows of seats and wide aisles, making it more spacious than the Tohoku Shinkansen. Speaking of Shinkansen, it is definitely Tokaido Shinkansen.

These Japanese Bullet trains are so fast and smooth and get you to your destination so comfortably. The entire time I was riding the train I was saying to myself. Why don't we have more of these in the USA. It is expensive  to ride the Bullet train but with a very small freeway and street  system, and a lot of people in Japan, this is the only way to travel. There are buses , Taxis, Trolleys, and regular Trains, but this Bullet train is the best !

Not even one bump. I loved this ride. Be sure to seek out this particular train, there are many trains that go this route but only one Shinkansen. It is the fastest and I'm guessing, the smoothest.
